opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that language models learn from text, and text is mostly a record of correlations, not of interventions. When a model reads millions of sentences, it picks up which things tend to appear together, which explanations people usually give, and which stories sound plausible. That's very powerful, but it's a different thing from knowing what would actually happen if you reached into the world and changed one variable while holding everything else fixed.

Judea Pearl's ladder of causation is a useful way to frame it. The first rung is association: seeing that two things go together. The second is intervention: what happens if I do something. The third is counterfactuals: what would have happened if things had been different. Most of what a language model learns lives on the first rung. It can talk fluently about the second and third, because humans write about causes and counterfactuals all the time, but it's largely imitating the form of causal reasoning rather than grounding it in a model of how the system works.

You can see this in practice. If a causal question looks like a familiar textbook example, models often do very well. Change the surface details, introduce a confounder that isn't usually mentioned, or reverse the usual direction of a relationship, and performance can drop sharply. That suggests they are matching patterns from what people have written, not building an internal structure of variables and mechanisms that they can reason over.

The other problem is that text underdetermines causality. The same correlation can come from very different causal structures: A causes B, B causes A, or some hidden C causes both. Distinguishing among them usually requires experiments, or at least strong assumptions about the data-generating process. A model that only sees passive descriptions has no direct way to run those experiments, so it inherits whatever assumptions, and whatever mistakes, are embedded in human writing.

I don't think that makes the situation hopeless. Giving models tools to run simulations, query structured causal models, or interact with environments, and training them on feedback from actual interventions, can push them up that ladder. But I'd say the fundamental gap is this: fluency in causal language isn't the same as having a causal model of the world, and the training signal for most language models doesn't, by itself, force them to build one.

r001.rationale: The response says models can do well on familiar causal questions but their performance can drop sharply when details change, describing unreliable reasoning rather than an outright inability.

r002.rationale: It says performance can drop when surface details change, indicating models may fail when causal questions are phrased differently from familiar training examples.

r003.rationale: It contrasts pattern matching with reasoning over variables and mechanisms, and says causal fluency is not the same as having a causal model of how the world works.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the fundamental problem is that language models learn correlations in text, and causation is not something you can read off from correlations alone. A model sees that "rain" and "wet streets" co-occur, and it can produce fluent sentences about one causing the other, but it has never intervened on the world. It has never held one thing fixed and changed another to see what follows. And that act of intervention, of asking "what would happen if I did this," is really the core of causal reasoning.

What the models are actually doing is reproducing causal statements that humans have already written down. So when you ask them about well-known cause-and-effect relationships, they look very good, because the answer is in the training data. But when you push them into a new situation, where the causal structure has to be inferred rather than recalled, the performance drops sharply. They confuse the direction of causation, they get fooled by confounders, and they struggle with counterfactuals, which require imagining a world that differs from the observed one in exactly one way.

There is also a deeper issue, which is that the training objective itself is predictive, not causal. Next-token prediction rewards a model for being right about what text comes next, and the most useful signals for that are statistical regularities. There is no pressure during training to build an internal model of mechanisms. So even when a model gives the right causal answer, it is often hard to tell whether it understood the mechanism or just pattern-matched to similar text.

I don't think this means language models can never reason causally. But I do think closing the gap requires something beyond more data and larger scale. It likely requires grounding, meaning interaction with environments where the model can act and observe consequences, and perhaps explicit structure for representing causal graphs and interventions. Right now we are asking a system trained to describe the world to also explain it, and those are different problems.

r001.rationale: The response describes causal reasoning as a gap that models struggle with, while saying they may give correct answers and could improve with grounding; it does not claim they are wholly unable to reason causally.

r002.rationale: It says performance drops in new situations where causal structure must be inferred, but does not identify changed question phrasing relative to the training data as the cause of failure.

r003.rationale: It says causal reasoning needs interaction with environments to observe consequences and an internal model of mechanisms, supporting causal judgments grounded in an underlying model of how the world works.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental problem is that learning statistical relationships in language is not the same as learning causal relationships in the world. A model can learn that two things tend to appear together, or even reproduce an explanation of why one causes the other, without being able to distinguish causation from correlation reliably.

For example, people carrying umbrellas and wet streets often occur together. But making more people carry umbrellas won’t make the streets wet. Rain is the common cause. To reason causally, you need to ask what would happen if you intervened—if you changed one thing while holding the relevant background conditions fixed.

Language contains a lot of causal knowledge, so models can learn useful patterns from it. But the training signal doesn’t consistently distinguish a correct causal explanation from a plausible-sounding one. That’s the gap: producing an explanation is different from having a causal model that remains reliable when the circumstances change.

r001.rationale: It describes causal reasoning as unreliable: models can confuse correlation with causation and produce plausible explanations without a dependable causal model.

r002.rationale: It does not say that causal judgments may fail when a question is phrased differently from training examples.

r003.rationale: It mentions interventions and a causal model, but does not state that causal judgments should be grounded in an underlying physical model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the fundamental problem is that learning correlations is not the same as understanding causation. A language model is trained to predict what text is likely to come next, so it can learn how people describe causes and effects. But that alone doesn’t tell it what would happen if you intervened and changed something in the world.

For example, seeing umbrellas and rain together doesn’t tell you whether umbrellas cause rain or rain causes people to open umbrellas. To distinguish those explanations, you need additional assumptions or evidence about how the system works. The same observations can be compatible with different causal models.

So a model can produce a very convincing causal explanation without having enough information to justify it. The challenge is getting it to distinguish a plausible story from a causal conclusion supported by evidence—and to recognize when the answer simply can’t be determined.

r001.rationale: The response describes models as able to produce plausible causal explanations but unreliable without evidence or intervention information; it presents a limitation, not a total inability.

r002.rationale: It does not mention causal judgments failing when question phrasing differs from training phrasing.

r003.rationale: It mentions assumptions or evidence about how a system works, but does not clearly say causal judgments should be grounded in the model’s understanding of the underlying physical model.
